prs.verdict_pattern: comment-then-approve: six inline comments across two days (2026-05-12, 2026-05-13) as text-less COMMENTED reviews, each a question or a nit; author answered every one (two with code changes in commit e4c4f49452 'PR #2713 review: single-chunk invariant, STORY-445 TODO, drop forensic ref', one with commit ea19ed5624 'introduce INVALID_CLASS', two with Notion stories STORY-445/STORY-461); Wade APPROVED 2026-05-18 with no text at commit ab8a7f758b. PR was later closed unmerged (base branch hwattention_sync).
prs.pr_level_notes: PR = pos_heap_v2, a new DMA (direct memory access) hugepage arena allocator for tron behind env var TRON_USE_ARENA_ALLOCATOR, plus HBM allocator FUSE stats, a design doc (doc/pos_heap_v2.md, 1152 lines), tests t_heap_v2 / t_alloc_contention / t_token_tree_refcount; 41 commits, 22 files, by bham0n. Wade reviewed code and comments, not process: he read the spec and compared it with the code (chunks[0] vs 'one or more chunks'), read comment text for stale/private references (for_claude/heap-profile.log), asked whether a workaround and its guarding test have a tracking story, nit-picked a sentinel that reuses a count constant (NUM_CLASSES) as an error value, and asked about Perfetto TRACE_EVENT instrumentation of the allocator paths. No comment on the 1152-line spec itself, the 41-commit history, the microbenchmark method, the PR body, or CI. None of the six comments is an instance of the existing 13 checks as written; the nearest is check 13 (constant naming), partial.

comments.concern: A code comment in expand() (the function that adds a hugepage chunk to the pool) describes a reversed free-list push order as a 'workaround for an unidentified bug' (first FPGA DMA hangs when the descriptor ring lands at a high offset); Wade asks whether a ticket or story tracks the follow-up investigation.

detection.trigger: An added comment or commit message contains a word such as 'workaround', 'unidentified', 'unknown bug', 'open question', 'follow-up', 'TODO' with no ticket id (STORY-nnn, issue #nnn) in the same comment block.
detection.procedure: grep the diff's added lines for workaround|unidentified|unknown|open question|follow-up|TODO|FIXME; for each hit, check the same comment block, the PR body and the commit message for a ticket reference (STORY-, #nnn, notion.so link); if none, ask for one.
detection.question: Does a ticket or story exist, and is its id written next to the workaround so the next reader can find the follow-up?

comments.quote: do we have a ticket/story tracking this for follow up?
comments.note: The hunk's own text supplies the trigger: 'Reproducible workaround for an unidentified bug' and 'See TODO: open question for follow-up' with no ticket id. Author answered STORY-445 and commit e4c4f49452 added 'TODO(STORY-445)' to the guarding test in t/t_heap_v2.cpp (the expand() comment in src/system/heap_v2.cpp was not changed by that commit).

comments.concern: A new TEST_CASE 'expand: first allocation comes from the lowest-offset hugepage' pins the workaround ordering as a tested contract; Wade asks whether that makes the workaround permanent or whether a story will pursue the root cause, and if so asks for a TODO in the test saying so.

detection.trigger: A new test unit whose header comment says it 'guards' or 'protects' a workaround, hack, or unexplained behavior (words: workaround, hang, unidentified, silently flipped).
detection.procedure: Read the TEST_CASE header comment and the production comment it cites; check whether either names a ticket or a plan to replace the test once the root cause is known; if not, ask whether the behavior is meant to be permanent and request a TODO(ticket) in the test.
detection.question: Is this test guarding a contract the team wants forever, or a temporary workaround that a ticket will remove, and does the test text say which?

comments.quote: so are we enshrining this work-around forever? Or will be create a story to pursue/understand/address it further? If so we should probably call that out here with a TODO or something.
comments.note: Related to check 1 in theme (a test row with no consumer beyond the test comment) but the trigger differs: this is an ordering assertion on a free-list head, not a numeric conversion row, and Wade's remedy is a TODO plus a tracking story rather than dropping the row. Author agreed ('the output of that work will be to put in a real test for the condition and remove this one') and commit e4c4f49452 added the TODO(STORY-445) block to this test.

comments.concern: The design spec says a pool can hold 'one or more chunks', but heap_start() and heap_size() (the functions that report the DMA heap range to the driver) read only pool.chunks[0]; Wade asks whether the spec is wrong or the functions are insufficient, noting expand() called twice would create more than one chunk.

detection.trigger: Production code indexes a collection with a fixed index ([0], .front(), .back()) or asserts non-empty only, while a design doc, Note or comment in the same PR says the collection can hold several elements.
detection.procedure: For each added `x[0]` / `.front()` / `.chunks.empty()` guard on a container, grep the PR's doc/*.md, Notes and header comments for the container's cardinality ('one or more', 'multiple', 'list of'); find every caller that can grow the container (here expand()) and count its call sites; if the doc allows N and the code handles 1, ask which is right and request an assert or a doc fix.
detection.question: If the container ever holds more than one element, is this read still correct, and if not, does an assert or the doc say that only one is allowed?

comments.quote:
the spec says a pool can have "one or more chunks"... but we only ever look at `chunks[0]` here and below in heap_size. So is the spec wrong? Or are these functions insufficient?

If `expand()` is called multiple times, we would create >1 chunk right?
comments.note: Wade cross-read doc/pos_heap_v2.md ('mmap that budget as one or more chunks') against the code. The hunk showed `TRON_ASSERT(!h->pool.chunks.empty(), ...)` then `return h->pool.chunks[0].base`. Commit e4c4f49452 replaced the non-empty assert with `TRON_ASSERT_EQ(h->pool.chunks.size(), 1u)` in both heap_start and heap_size and added a comment explaining that internals support multi-chunk but the VFIO IOMMU map and dispatch surface assume one chunk.

comments.concern: A header comment tells the reader to see a file for_claude/heap-profile.log that exists only on the author's machine and is not in the change set; Wade points out nobody else can open it.

detection.trigger: An added comment, Note or doc line names a file path (contains '/' and an extension, or a directory such as for_claude/, tmp/, /home/, /var/tmp/) that is not under the repository or not in the PR's file list.
detection.procedure: Extract every path-like token from the diff's added comment lines; for each, run `git ls-files <path>` at HEAD and check the PR file list; report every path that resolves nowhere.
detection.question: Can a reader of the repository at HEAD open the file this comment points to?

comments.quote: `for_claude/heap-profile.log` probably won't exist for anybody else but you ;p?
comments.note: Check 9 covers machine-local paths and log names but only inside PR-body Status/Verification/Tests/Results sections; this hit is in a header comment, so the trigger as written does not fire. Author deleted the reference in commit e4c4f49452 ('Uncomment for fragmentation research.').

comments.concern: class_for() (maps a size and alignment to a size-class index) returns NUM_CLASSES, the count of classes, as its error value; Wade says reusing a count as an error sentinel is non-intuitive and suggests a named INVALID_CLASS constant (nit).

detection.trigger: A function returns, or a comment says it returns, an existing constant whose role is a count or a bound (NUM_*, *_COUNT, size(), MAX_*) as a failure or 'not found' signal, with no dedicated named sentinel.
detection.procedure: grep the diff's added lines for `return NUM_` / `return MAX_` / `== NUM_` and for comments containing 'sentinel'; check whether a dedicated constant (INVALID_*, NONE, NOT_FOUND) exists in the same header; if not, suggest one.
detection.question: Does the returned value's name say 'failure' at the call site, or does it say 'count' and leave the reader to know the convention?

comments.note: The hunk's comment already says 'Returns NUM_CLASSES as a sentinel'. Check 13 is about constant stems in a family with value suffixes; here the issue is a constant used in a role its name does not state, so same theme, different trigger. Note the file already had `constexpr uint32_t INVALID_IDX = ~0u;` in the same hunk as a model. Author added `constexpr uint8_t INVALID_CLASS = 0xff;` in commit ea19ed5624 (constexpr, not #define as Wade sketched).

comments.concern: Wade asks whether the allocator paths (drain_reserves() walk over all arenas, allocate, deallocate) should emit Perfetto TRACE_EVENTs so their cost can be measured, and notes there is no 'memory' Perfetto category at all; explicitly no action required.

detection.trigger: The PR adds a new subsystem or hot path (allocator, scheduler step, loop over all N items under a lock) with no TRACE_EVENT / TRON_CHECKPOINT / counter in any added line.
detection.procedure: grep the diff's added src/ lines for TRACE_EVENT|TRON_CHECKPOINT; grep h/common/perfetto.hpp for a category matching the subsystem name; if both absent, ask (as a non-blocking question) whether the walk/loop cost should be observable and whether a category is missing.
detection.question: Could an operator measure the cost of this new path in a trace today, and if not, is that a deliberate choice?

comments.quote: wouldn't it be useful to have some TRACE_EVENTs we can gather metrics across these memory paths? Might be worth knowing the cost of walks like this, etc. I noticed we don't even currently have a "memory" category defined for Perfetto. That seems like a gap?
comments.note: Wade read h/common/perfetto.hpp (or its category list) outside the diff to state no 'memory' category exists. He wrote 'No action needed, just inquiring.' Author confirmed the gap (10 categories, none for memory, no allocator emits TRACE_EVENT), flagged the ~20 ns/op hot-path cost as a reason to keep such a category off by default, and filed STORY-461. No code change in this PR.

Wade reviewed code, not process: all 7 inline comments are on src/. Themes: signedness of count/size variables (4 of 7 comments, one question then three one-line suggestion blocks that pin the fix after the author only partly applied it), a comment-vs-code name mismatch (ares_fields vs wres_fields), a pasted GPT review finding about a helper not honoring its own comment contract (first_desc stays 0 for legacy requests), and one praise. He did not ask for tests, did not comment on the PR body, did not comment on commit history (10 commits incl. 3 merges and a 'formatting' commit) and did not comment on the hot-path risk the Cursor summary flags. Verified at head 17c6e0117d: all suggestions applied (uint64_t res_per_block/res_bytes_per_block/pad_bytes at :1482/:1507/:1509, comment says wres_fields at :1112, first_desc also set from the first activation descriptor at :1428 in commit 381ed8ed4a).

comments.concern: The three local counters expected_blocks, res_per_block and res_bytes_per_block (block and result-word counts for one FPGA request) plus pad_bytes are declared as signed int / int64_t although they can never be negative, so Wade asks whether an unsigned type is the right one.

detection.trigger: The diff adds or keeps a local variable, parameter or struct member of signed type (int, int64_t, long) whose name denotes a count, size, index or byte length (suffixes/words: count, cnt, blocks, bytes, size, per_block, idx, num_).
detection.procedure: For each such declaration, read every assignment and every producer function: if the producers' out-parameters or return types are unsigned (grep the file for 'uint64_t& <name>' or the callee's signature), and no code path assigns a negative value or compares against < 0, the signed type is a narrowing/sign mismatch. Also check the consumer struct field type (here rxinfo::results_per_block) with grep over h/ and src/.
detection.question: Can this variable ever legitimately hold a negative value, and do its producers and consumers already use an unsigned type?

comments.quote: these 3 variables below are never expected to be negative right? Wouldn't `uint` make more sense for those? Same for `pad_bytes`?
comments.note: At commit 40e4cea98609 (the review's commit) worker.cpp:1693-1696 read 'int expected_blocks = 0; int res_per_block = 0; int res_bytes_per_block = 0; int64_t pad_bytes = 0;' while the producer out-params at :566-568 were already 'uint64_t&'. The digest shows the comment against head 17c6e0117d where these are uint64_t (:1695-1698), so the author applied it. 'uint' means unsigned type in general, the fix used uint64_t. The author applied it to the locals but left three helper parameters signed, which produced the three suggestion-block comments the next day.

comments.concern: Wade relays a GPT review finding: write_tx_descriptors (the new helper that writes the TX DMA descriptor chain) sets first_desc only in the metadata loop, so for legacy requests (num_metadata_wds == 0) it returns 0 and fill_rxinfo records a wrong tx_desc_start_idx, contradicting the helper's own comment contract.

detection.trigger: The diff extracts a helper that returns or writes an out-value (here first_desc) and its header comment states what the value is ('first descriptor index'), while the value is initialised to a sentinel and assigned inside only one of several loops/branches.
detection.procedure: For each out-value of a new helper, list every assignment site and the branch condition guarding it. Enumerate the callers' input classes (here attn_req true/false -> num_metadata_wds 0 or >0) and check whether some class skips every assignment, leaving the init sentinel. Then find the consumer of the value (grep for the struct field it is stored into, rxinfo.tx_desc_start_idx, and its readers in the RX worker / debug dump) to state the consequence. Also compare with the pre-refactor code at BASE to see whether the old inline code set it on that path.
detection.question: Is there an input class for which the helper returns its initial sentinel instead of the value its comment promises, and who reads that value?

comments.quote:
GPT had this to say about `first_desc`:

>   **1. Low**: write_tx_descriptors() does not actually return the first TX descriptor for legacy requests.

comments.concern: The new helper fill_rxinfo (fills the rxinfo ring entry the RX worker drains) takes res_per_block as int while the caller's value is uint64_t; Wade suggests uint64_t.

detection.trigger: A new or changed function parameter has a signed integer type while every caller passes a variable of an unsigned (wider) type, or the earlier review already asked to make the same quantity unsigned.

comments.concern: In monitor_and_wait (the mwaitx spin-wait helper) the new threshold computation calls ns_to_cycles on every entry, and Wade asks to test the `0 == wait_cycles` indefinite-wait case first so that callers who asked for an indefinite wait do not pay that cost.

detection.trigger: A hunk in a hot-path function (a wait, poll, enqueue or per-command routine) adds a computation (function call, division, static initializer) before a branch, and one branch of the following if/else chain does not need that computation.
detection.procedure: Read the whole function at HEAD. For each branch of the if/else chain after the added computation, check whether the branch uses the computed value. If a branch does not, and that branch is a common call pattern (grep callers for the special argument, here `wait_for_not_event(..., 0)` or timeout 0), propose reordering so the branch that does not need the value is tested first. Check whether the computation is `static const` (one-time init plus a guard check per call) versus per-call; state the actual per-call cost.
detection.question: Does a branch that runs without needing the newly added computation get evaluated only after that computation is paid?

comments.quote: this is maybe a nit... but it seems like we should check for the `else if (0 == wait_cycles)` case first? This change is forcing a call to `ns_to_cycles` every time through here now, even if the caller asked for an indefinite wait.

Because the variable is `static const`, ns_to_cycles runs once per process, not every call; the per-call cost is the static-init guard check. Wade's 'every time' is an over-statement that nobody corrected. Author replied 'seems like a reasonable change'; Bill replied that ns_to_cycles could be made cheap and he would patch it. The branch order is unchanged at head b8739108f7, so the agreed change was not made in this PR.

comments.concern: Self-reply adding a mechanism concern: push_back beyond capacity on a std::vector invalidates references to existing elements, while std::deque keeps references valid; relevant because the loop holds a reference to the top frame while pushing child frames.

detection.trigger: A function takes a reference or pointer to an element of a std::vector (back(), operator[], iterator) and the same function calls push_back/emplace_back/insert/resize on that vector while the reference is still live.
detection.procedure: In the changed function, find every 'auto& x = vec.back()' or element reference; then find every growth call on the same vector between that line and the last use of x. If one exists on a path with no 'continue', 'break' or return before the next use, it is a dangling reference. Here: 'frame_t& f = stk.back();' at line 1403, 'stk.push_back' at 1852 followed by 'continue', so f is not used after the push.
detection.question: Is any reference into this vector used after a call that can grow the vector?

prs.pr_level_notes: PR by mcherba: DMA coalescence for KV hardware-cache-block transfers (FPGA attention KV path). Areas: src/tron/gof.cpp (GOF = group-of-four-tokens transfer unit, populate + xfer), h/tron/models/model.hpp (cooperative drain / rodeo dispatch), h/pos/dma_tracker.hpp (in-flight DMA bookkeeping), src/pos/fake.cpp (fake device), tests t_dma_tracker / t_phase1_integration / t_llama_unit. Wade reviewed CODE and TEST DESIGN, not process: performance of the prefill and decode hot paths (allocation, memset, sort, redundant gather, duplicated assert), concurrency safety (buffer freed under live DMA, widened v_buf race, decode budget escalation), duplication of a safety-critical ordering, an alignment bug, and two coverage gaps (fake discards descriptors; tests bypass the production drain). The 2026-09-08 comments use a formal register ('Coverage gap:', 'Please extend an existing CI suite', 'I have not observed ... failure') consistent with Claude-assisted drafting (CONTEXT.md notes he pastes Claude review items on this PR). Head evidence (read, not inferred): commit subjects 'Improve V path handling to reduce extra work as per ...#issuecomment-5498556672', 'Replaced cooperative drain vectors with bounded std::array batches and immediate empty-queue exits', 'Consolidate prepared-transfer grouping and dispatch into one helper', 'Address Review feedback'; at 7f80aa17da gof.cpp:249-252 uses std::array descriptor arrays and comment 'without a sort', gof.cpp:352 alignas(HWCACHEBLOCK_ALIGN_BYTES) v_scratch, gof.cpp:438 dispatch_prepared_gof_xfers, model.hpp:1166 gof_prompt_sized_pass flag, fake.cpp:376-390 xfer_n_blocks captures descriptors when fake_dma_capture_enabled, t_llama_unit.cpp:1020 'production GOF drain handles fanout layers and reservation gaps', t_phase1_integration.cpp:1024 'partial odd-head GOF run keeps fixed K and V strides' using fake_dma_capture_guard. So every inline item was adopted; no author replies exist in the digest. The abandon-in-destructor item from the conversation comment is NOT visible at head (no 'abandon' in dma_tracker.hpp/.cpp at 7f80aa17da): Insufficient data on whether it was discussed elsewhere.

comments.concern: Wade noticed the V-populate path (the code that gathers value-cache rows into the DMA staging buffer) does far more work than the path it replaces, ran a Claude review on the PR, and relays five items: a queued batch pending_xfer (the record of one in-flight DMA) freed without abandon() releases the buffer while the DMA still reads it; decode passes with 32 or more users wrongly get the prompt-sized drain budget; hot-path costs (32x gather, memset, mallocs, sort, duplicated assert); per-shard batch buffers under branch fanout; two consistency nits (missing n_kv_heads assert, % FETCHERS_PER_DEVICE vs % dev->num_fetchers spelling).

detection.trigger: The diff adds a struct that owns a buffer handed to an asynchronous engine (DMA descriptor, in-flight transfer record) and the only release path is a manual call (abandon(), clear()) rather than the destructor; or adds a budget/eligibility predicate that tests a token count where the comment speaks of pass shape (prompt vs decode).
detection.procedure: Read the new struct in h/pos/dma_tracker.hpp and every site that constructs or drops it (grep pending_xfer, push(, abandon(, clear(); list each path where the object can be destroyed before completion and check whether the destructor releases the buffer. For the budget: read the predicate (gof_jobs_span.size() >= hwkv_coalesce_tokens) and the comment above it, then ask which pass shapes satisfy it. For the nits: grep the sibling writers of the same storage for the assert and the modulus spelling and compare the new path.
detection.question: Is there a path where this object is dropped before the DMA completes without the destructor releasing the buffer, and do the new path's asserts and spellings match every sibling writer of the same storage?

Other patterns inside this one comment: decode-budget-gated-on-token-count-not-pass-shape, perf-extra-work-on-hot-path, batch-buffer-per-shard-under-fanout, assert-parity-with-sibling-writers, spelling-parity-with-sibling-path. Outcome evidence read at head 7f80aa17da: commit subject 'Improve V path handling to reduce extra work as per ...#issuecomment-5498556672' cites this comment; model.hpp:1166 adds bool gof_prompt_sized_pass (pass-shape gate); gof.cpp:414 batch path now carries TRON_ASSERT(n_kv_heads <= HW_MAX_KV_HEADS). 'Consistency nits' is Wade's own severity word for the last bullet.

comments.concern: xfer_gofs (the new batched GOF transfer function) runs about 4608 times per long prefill and does avoidable per-call work: a memset of up to 128 KiB the populate loops overwrite anyway, six heap vectors where the sibling single-GOF function uses stack arrays, a std::sort that order-of-emission makes unnecessary, and a piece-major V gather that calls v_head_fn 32x more than the path it replaces while widening a pre-existing cross-layer v_buf race.

detection.trigger: A new function on a per-token or per-layer path (called from prefill/decode loops) contains heap containers (std::vector), a whole-buffer memset/fill, a std::sort, or a nested loop that re-runs a gather per inner element, where a sibling function on the same path uses fixed arrays or does the gather once.
detection.procedure: Find the callers of the new function (grep its name in src/ and h/) and count calls per forward pass from the loop structure (layers x GOFs). Inside the function list every std::vector, memset/std::fill, std::sort and lambda call inside a loop. For each, read the sibling function that handled the singleton case (xfer_gof, gof::populate) and compare: fixed std::array bounded by a constant, zeroing limited to padded regions, order-by-construction instead of sort, gather once per (pos,head). For a shared scratch (v_buf) check what key it is indexed by versus the key of the busy flag (staging_busy) and name the race window.
detection.question: Does the hot-path function do per-call work (allocation, zeroing, sorting, repeated gathers) that its singleton sibling already avoids with bounded stack storage and emission order?

comments.quote: xfer_gofs does some avoidable per-call work on the prefill critical path (a 4096-token 36-layer prefill runs this ~4608 times):
comments.note: Wade computed 4096/128 tokens... x 36 layers = 4608 calls and ~576 MB dead stores (4608 x 128 KiB) - arithmetic from the hunk plus the constants. Also names the exact sibling helper (shuffle_v_entry_padded) and the 1024-vs-32 gather count. Secondary pattern in the same comment: shared-scratch-race-widened (v_buf keyed per gal/position but staging_busy keyed per gal/layer). Head 7f80aa17da evidence: gof.cpp:249-252 std::array<...,max_specs> bases/fetchers/qdatas/qlens, comment at :244-247 'without a sort or generic coalescing pass', std::fill only on padded regions (:294,:300,:323), no memset. So all three bullets were adopted.

comments.concern: The decode drain helpers help_drain_gof and wait_for_coop_gof construct and reserve a std::vector before checking whether the queue is empty, adding a malloc/free per spin iteration per worker per layer per token where the old code allocated nothing; gof_rodeo_impl_batch repeats an assert fire_gof_rodeo already made (TRON_ASSERT is live in release, 8 std::function calls instead of 4); and the prompt-sized-pass predicate counts token jobs, so a decode pass with 32 or more sessions gets the escalated budget at the pre-barrier idle point.

detection.trigger: A diff replaces a zero-allocation loop (try_dequeue into a local) with a container that is allocated before the empty check, in a function called from a spin-wait or per-token path; or a diff adds a TRON_ASSERT that re-evaluates a callback already asserted by the caller on identical inputs; or a comment says 'generation keeps X' while the predicate tests a count that decode can also satisfy.
detection.procedure: grep the callers of help_drain_gof / wait_for_coop_gof (hw_q_released_layer spin, begin_attention_job) and state the call frequency. Compare the removed lines (gof_coop_task task; try_dequeue loop) with the added lines (std::vector constructed before try_dequeue). For the duplicated assert, follow fire_gof_rodeo into gof_rodeo_impl_batch and list the asserts on the same inputs; check whether TRON_ASSERT compiles into release builds. For the predicate, read the comment and compute which decode batch sizes make gof_jobs_span.size() >= hwkv_coalesce_tokens true.
detection.question: On the per-token spin path, does the new code allocate or re-assert where the old code did not, and does the budget predicate admit decode passes the comment says it excludes?

comments.quote: the std::vector<gof_coop_task> is constructed and reserved before checking whether the coop queue has anything. These run from the hw_q_released_layer spin and begin_attention_job — per worker, per layer, per decode token
comments.note: Three patterns in one comment: perf-avoidable-alloc-on-hot-path (primary), duplicate-assert-on-release-path (TRON_ASSERT stays in release, so cost is real), decode-budget-gated-on-token-count-not-pass-shape (also in 5498556672). He proposes the exact remedy: try-dequeue first, early-return on empty, fixed std::array bounded by max(4, coalesce_gofs). Head 7f80aa17da evidence: commit 'Replaced cooperative drain vectors with bounded std::array batches and immediate empty-queue exits in model.hpp'; hunk under 3960538961 shows std::array<gof_coop_task, drain_capacity> tasks; if (!try_dequeue(tasks[0])) return; and gof_prompt_sized_pass flag at model.hpp:1166; only one kv_complete_fn(layer) assert remains (model.hpp:3089).

comments.concern: The sort/group/dispatch block, which carries the staging-lifetime-critical ordering reservation.commit() -> guard.commit() -> tracker.push(pending_xfer{...}) from PR #3928, now exists in four near-verbatim copies across gof.cpp and model.hpp, with twin request structs and two copies of the run-grouping predicate; a future edit that misses one copy becomes a silent staging-lifetime bug rather than a compile error.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a second (or further) copy of a statement sequence whose order is documented as safety-critical (a comment near one copy explains why the ordering matters), or adds a struct that is another struct plus one member, or repeats a predicate lambda in two files.
detection.procedure: Take the ordered call sequence from the hunk (reservation.commit, guard.commit, tracker.push) and grep each name across h/ and src/; list every site where the three appear in sequence and note which sites keep the explanatory comment. Diff the two request structs field by field. Diff the grouping predicates (same layer, consecutive gof_in_shard, same window, same shard). Check git log / PR history for where the ordering was introduced (here #3928) to confirm it is safety-critical.
detection.question: If someone changes the commit ordering, the grouping predicate or a pending_xfer field in one copy, does the compiler or any test catch the other copies?

comments.quote: All four carry the same safety-critical sequence from the staging-lifetime work in #3928: reservation.commit() -> guard.commit() -> tracker.push(pending_xfer{...}), where the ordering is what keeps staging alive under submitted descriptors
comments.note: Wade cross-referenced two files and the originating PR #3928 to establish why the ordering is safety-critical, and noted the explanatory comment survives only next to some copies (comment-lost-in-copy). He did not propose the helper's shape; the author did. Head 7f80aa17da evidence: commit 'Consolidate prepared-transfer grouping and dispatch into one helper'; gof.cpp:438 void dispatch_prepared_gof_xfers(std::span<prepared_gof_xfer> ...) called from gof.cpp:557 and model.hpp:3111 - so the four copies became one helper.

comments.concern: The singleton V-gather scratch introduced at gof.cpp:436 is an ordinary stack std::array that is passed through v_head_into_fn to page::get_v(), which stores with _mm256_store_si256 (an AVX2 aligned store needing 32-byte alignment); the compiled function can place it 16 bytes off, so singleton decode submissions and singleton remainders can fault or silently corrupt; fix is alignas(HWCACHEBLOCK_ALIGN_BYTES) like the batch scratch plus a test that drives the real gather.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a stack or member buffer (std::array, C array) with no alignas and passes its pointer into a callback or function whose implementation uses an aligned SIMD store/load (_mm256_store_si256, _mm512_store_*, _tile_*), or the sibling buffer in the same file carries alignas and the new one does not.
detection.procedure: For each new buffer, follow the pointer to every consumer (grep the callback name v_head_into_fn; read page::get_v in the KV cache header) and grep the consumer for aligned intrinsics. Compare with sibling buffers in the same file (grep alignas). Compile the changed function and inspect the stack frame offset of the buffer (objdump/-S), or build a UBSan (-fsanitize=alignment) reproducer that calls the gather's exact intrinsics with the misaligned destination.
detection.question: Does any consumer of this buffer require an alignment stronger than the buffer's declared alignment?

comments.quote:
This singleton V-gather scratch is insufficiently aligned.
     gof.cpp:436 introduces an ordinary stack array, then passes it through v_head_into_fn to page::get_v(). That gather uses _mm256_store_si256, requiring 32-byte alignment.
comments.note: Only comment in this PR where Wade reports having run something: 'Compiling the changed function confirmed that its scratch can be misaligned by 16 bytes. A small UBSan reproducer ... fails with that alignment'. He also warns the bug is masked by optimized Clang ('can mask the violation by fusing instructions'), i.e. tests on the normal build will not catch it - hence the ask for a test that exercises the real gather through singleton population. The static part (alignas missing where the sibling at :417 has it) is reviewable by code reading alone; the proof needed a compile. Head 7f80aa17da evidence: gof.cpp:352 alignas(HWCACHEBLOCK_ALIGN_BYTES) std::array<bf16, HW_BAKED_HEAD_SIZE> v_scratch; and :417 alignas on the batch scratch.

comments.concern: The new batch tests cannot detect wrong DMA destinations because the fake device's xfer_n_blocks (src/pos/fake.cpp) discards every descriptor argument; the tests check staging bytes and descriptor counts only, both start at GOF index zero, so wrong HBM bases, fetchers, source offsets or lengths would pass; Wade asks for an existing CI suite to capture descriptors at the transfer boundary and compare coalesced versus singleton transfers, with nonzero indices, partial windows and page-boundary runs.

detection.trigger: A new test asserts on a count, a size or a sample of intermediate values (descriptor_count, batch->size, selected staging entries) while the production call under test hands its real output (descriptors, addresses, lengths) to a fake or stub that ignores them; and every new case uses the zero/first index.
detection.procedure: Read the test's REQUIRE/CHECK lines and list what they observe. Follow the call under test (shard::xfer_gofs) to the device entry point (xfer_n_blocks) and read the fake implementation in src/pos/fake.cpp: do the arguments reach any storage a test can read? Enumerate inputs the tests vary (GOF indices, window fullness, page boundary) and list which equivalence classes are absent. Ask what a plausible bug (off-by-one base, wrong fetcher, wrong length) would change in the observed values.
detection.question: If the production code emitted the wrong destination address, fetcher, offset or length, which assertion in the new tests would fail?

comments.quote: `pos_fake::xfer_n_blocks` (`src/pos/fake.cpp:336–346`) discards every descriptor argument. These tests inspect selected staging values and descriptor counts, so incorrect HBM bases, fetchers, source offsets, or transfer lengths would still pass.
comments.note: Fit with check 3 is partial: check 3's theme is 'the assertion that would catch the bug never executes'; here the assertion executes but observes a quantity the bug does not change, with the fake as the sink. Wade's finding shape: bold 'Coverage gap:' headline, the mechanism fact with file:line, the equivalence-class list the tests lack (nonzero index, partial window, page boundary), the ask 'extend an existing CI suite' (not a new file), and a closing 'the current packing assertions do not establish that contract'. He also asks for a differential oracle (coalesced == singleton bytes at the same HBM locations). Head 7f80aa17da evidence: fake.cpp:376-390 xfer_n_blocks now records {dev->idx, bases[i], fetchers[i], ...} into fake_dma_captured_transfers under fake_dma_capture_enabled; t_phase1_integration.cpp:790 fake_dma_capture_guard, :1024 'partial odd-head GOF run keeps fixed K and V strides'.

comments.concern: The changed cooperative rodeo orchestration (help_drain_gof batching, fire_gof_rodeo_batch, dispatch_prepared_gof_xfers grouping and reservation handoff) is not exercised by any test: the new tests call shard::xfer_gofs directly and the existing 'gof rodeo populates and xfers to shard' test invokes population and transfer by hand; Wade asks for cases through the production drain path (mixed shards and layers, a reservation collision gap, branch fanout) asserting each target gets its KV exactly once, skipped positions stay untouched, and the forward-end drain finishes before scheduler-owned job storage is rebuilt.

detection.trigger: The diff changes an orchestration function (a drain, dispatch or grouping routine) and the tests added or cited by the PR call a lower-level function that the orchestration wraps, or set up state by hand instead of calling the production entry point.
detection.procedure: List the functions the diff changed in h/tron/models/model.hpp (help_drain_gof, wait_for_coop_gof, fire_gof_rodeo_batch, gof_rodeo_impl_batch) and grep t/ for each name; for each test hit read whether it calls the production entry point or re-implements its steps. List the branches inside the orchestration (single vs batch, reservation collision, fanout, mixed layers) and for each name the test that reaches it or write 'none'. Identify the lifetime contract the orchestration protects (drain finishes before job storage is rebuilt) and check whether any assertion observes it.
detection.question: Which test reaches the changed orchestration function through its production caller, and which assertion fails if a GOF is lost, delivered twice, or completed before the drain finishes?

comments.quote: The added tests call `shard::xfer_gofs` directly. Even the existing test named "gof rodeo populates and xfers to shard" manually invokes population and transfer. Those cases do not exercise the new cooperative batching path
comments.note: Same finding shape as 3960538177: 'Coverage gap:' headline, named scenarios, 'Please extend an existing CI suite', then the explicit disclaimer 'These are missing safety-contract checks; I have not observed a lost-GOF or premature-completion failure in the implementation' - he separates a coverage finding from a claimed bug. Note he read the existing test by name to show it also bypasses the path (test-name-promises-more-than-it-exercises). Head 7f80aa17da evidence: t_llama_unit.cpp:1020 TEST_CASE 'production GOF drain handles fanout layers and reservation gaps' with gof_indices{2,3,4} (nonzero), n_layers = 2, built on gof_test_model state - matches his asks (fanout, reservation gap, nonzero indices).

prs.verdict_pattern: Five COMMENTED reviews, each carrying one inline comment, posted within 17 minutes on commit d306b805ce; then APPROVED with no text 9 minutes later on the fix-up head c502e4d61a ('Review feedback' commit). Approved although one of his concerns (NaN/inf handling in the comparison) got no reply and no code change; another (ktok test update) was answered by the author with an explanation and accepted as-is.
prs.pr_level_notes: PR by mcherba, base branch hwattention_sync (a feature branch, not main). Subject: the FPGA hardware-attention debug comparison path (compare hardware V readback results against the software reference), moving relerr/abserr/comberr error helpers from h/common/numerics/bf16.hpp to h/common/util.hpp, a ktok (token count field in the attention command metadata) formula change in src/pos/worker.cpp, and +184/-70 lines in t/t_hwattention_replay.cpp. Wade reviewed code hunks only: dead commented-out code, a now-unused include, a stale log label, NaN/inf special-value handling dropped by a refactor, and a production formula that tests mirror. He did not comment on the PR body, the 7-commit history with typo'd subjects, test structure, or CI. He is a co-developer of the hwattention tests ('I already have those changes staged'). All five comments were made from the diff hunks plus knowledge of sibling files; none needed a run.

comments.concern: The hunk comments out the `if (pdc + 1 == dev->num_fetchers)` guard around wait_for_hbm_vwrite_complete (the wait for the FPGA HBM V-cache write) instead of deleting it; Wade asks to delete the commented-out lines.

detection.trigger: An added line in the diff is a comment whose text is syntactically code (starts with `// if`, `// }`, `// <identifier>(`), or a removed code line reappears as an added `//`-prefixed line in the same hunk.
detection.procedure: For each hunk, compare removed lines with added lines after stripping a leading `//`; also grep the added lines for `^\s*//\s*(if|for|while|}|[A-Za-z_]+\()`. Confirm the commented text is not a prose comment by checking it parses as C++.
detection.question: Is this added comment line a piece of code that the PR disabled rather than an explanation, and does nothing in the PR body say it is kept on purpose?

comments.quote: can probably just remove the commented lines
comments.note: Verified: at d306b805ce h/pos/hwattention.hpp:703-706 has `// if (pdc + 1 == dev->num_fetchers) {` ... `//}` and a second commented-out old wait call below the loop. At the approved head c502e4d61a both are gone and replaced by a prose comment: 'wait after every transfer for now. This is needed to work around a chip hang and should be reduced once we have an updated bitfile.' Matches PR body line 'Add workaround to avoid HBM hang issue on v-cache transfers'.

comments.concern: The PR adds `#include "common/numerics/bf16.hpp"` to self_attention.hpp, but the same PR moved the error helpers (relerr, abserr, comberr) out of bf16.hpp into util.hpp, so the include is now unused; Wade asks whether it can go.

detection.trigger: The diff adds an `#include` line to a file, and the same PR removes definitions from the included header (the header appears in the file list with net negative lines) or moves them elsewhere.
detection.procedure: For each added `#include "X"` line, list the symbols the including file uses that X defines at HEAD (grep the names X declares at HEAD against the including file). If the set is empty, or every symbol is now declared by another header the file already includes (here common/util.hpp), the include is unused.
detection.question: Does the including file, at HEAD, use any symbol that only this newly added header provides?

comments.quote: don't need this bf16.hpp include now right?
comments.note: Verified: commit subject 'move relerr, abserr, and the combination call into h/common/util.hpp'; file list shows bf16.hpp +0 -31 and util.hpp +33 -0. At d306b805ce line 5 of self_attention.hpp is the bf16.hpp include and line 6 already includes common/util.hpp. At c502e4d61a the bf16.hpp include is removed (git diff d306b805ce..c502e4d61a shows only that line removed in the include block). Author reply: 'yup. I missed removing it.'

comments.concern: The debug log line still labels the printed value `HW O` (the normalized attention output), but the variable now printed is `hw_Ra_val`, the un-normalized accumulator Ra, which only becomes O after division by SUME (the softmax denominator); Wade asks why the label was not updated.

detection.trigger: A hunk renames or re-derives a variable (here `hw_O_val` -> `hw_Ra_val`, dropping the `/ *hw_sume` division) while a format string, log label, comment or identifier in the same or an adjacent unchanged line keeps the old name or the old quantity.
detection.procedure: For each renamed or re-derived variable in the diff, list the string literals, comments and identifiers within the same statement block that mention the old name or old quantity (grep the old stem, e.g. `O`, `HW O`, in the lines around the hunk at HEAD). Check whether the semantic relation stated by the old label still holds for the new value (here O = Ra / SUME, so Ra is not O).
detection.question: Does every label, format string and comment next to the changed variable describe the quantity that is now computed, not the one computed before the change?

comments.quote: why are you calling this `HW O` if you're printing the Ra value? We don't have an `O` until we divide Ra by SUME, right?
comments.note: The fact Wade relied on is visible in the hunk: the removed line `float hw_O_val = (static_cast<float>(hw_head[i])) / *hw_sume;` divided by SUME, the added line `float hw_Ra_val = (static_cast<float>(hw_head[i]));` does not, and the format string on the next line still says 'HW O:'. Verified at c502e4d61a:644 the string reads 'HW Ra:'. Commit subject in this PR: 'shift to checking vs Ra and not O. v_stars are NOT scaled values.' Check 5 covers a test name contradicting assertions; the same theme (a label says one thing, the code does another) but the trigger as written (TEST_CASE/SECTION name) does not fire on a log string in production debug code.

comments.concern: The production formula for the ktok metadata field (token count within the 128-token page) changes from `((acmd_len - 1) % 128) + 1` to `(acmd_len % 128) + 1`; Wade asks that the tests that write the same field (t_hwattention, t_hwattention_replay) be updated to match, or offers to do it himself after merge.

detection.trigger: A hunk in src/ or h/ changes an arithmetic formula that assigns a hardware command field or a protocol value, and the same field name is assigned in one or more test files that are not in the diff.
detection.procedure: Take the assigned field name (here `fields.ktok`) and grep t/ for every assignment of it. For each hit compare the test's formula, after substituting the test's local variable definitions (e.g. num_tokens = token_idx + 1), with the new production formula. List tests whose formula is not equivalent, and tests the PR touches that still carry the old form.
detection.question: After this production formula change, does every test that assigns the same field compute the same value for the same token index, and is each such test either updated in this PR or shown to be already equivalent?

comments.quote: this should be updated in the t_hwattention / t_hwattention_replay tests as well... else I can do it after you merge this I guess (I already have those changes staged)
comments.note: Author answered that t_hwattention_replay already matches: 'in t_hwattention_replay, we set num_tokens to be token_idx+1, then subtract off one here. that is correct behior, if confusing.' Verified at c502e4d61a: t/t_hwattention_replay.cpp:391 `num_tokens = token_idx + 1` and :549 `ktok = ((num_tokens - 1) % 128) + 1`, so ktok = (token_idx % 128) + 1; t/t_hwattention.cpp:1292 keeps `((num_tokens - 1) % 128) + 1` and :825 a literal 128; neither test file changed between d306b805ce and c502e4d61a for this. Whether the worker's acmd_len equals a token index (so the two forms agree) is not verified here. Wade approved after the explanation without replying.

comments.concern: The refactor replaced an explicit NaN/inf special case (which set the difference to infinity so a NaN or inf mismatch counted as a failure) with a call to comberr; Wade asks whether NaN/inf still need handling so that the hardware-versus-software comparison cannot produce a false pass.

detection.trigger: A hunk removes lines containing std::isnan, std::isfinite, std::isinf or a comment about NaN/inf (here 'to prevent false passes') and replaces the computation with a call to a helper, and the result of the helper feeds a `>` or `<` comparison against a tolerance.
detection.procedure: Read the helper at HEAD (here comberr/abserr/relerr in h/common/util.hpp). Trace what it returns for NaN and inf inputs. Then evaluate the consuming comparison with that return value: `NaN > tolerance` is false in C++, so a NaN result does not take the failure branch. Compare with what the removed code did for the same inputs. Cite the repository NaN rule (AGENTS.md: treat NaN as corruption) if present at that date.
detection.question: For a NaN or inf value on either side of the comparison, does the new code still reach the mismatch branch, as the removed code did?

comments.quote: also, don't we still need to consider nan / inf values? In order for the comparisons to be trust-worthy?
comments.note: No reply from the author in the digest, and h/common/util.hpp is identical between d306b805ce and c502e4d61a. Verified mechanism at d306b805ce h/common/util.hpp:271-282: abserr returns quiet_NaN when either input is NaN, and infinity for an inf mismatch (0 when both inf and equal); relerr (:259-268) has no NaN branch. The consumer at self_attention.hpp:642-643 tests `(abs_err > abs_tolerance) || (rel_err > rel_tolerance)`; for a NaN both comparisons are false, so mismatch_count is not incremented. The removed code set diff to infinity for any NaN/non-finite value, which did count. So Wade's concern holds by reading: a NaN on either side passes silently at the approved head. Wade approved anyway, 9 minutes after this reply.

prs.verdict_pattern: Many one-comment COMMENTED reviews in one sitting (11 reviews in 90 minutes on 2026-03-17, each carrying a single inline comment, no review body), then one more inline comment the next day and an APPROVED review with no text 5 minutes later at 8e19ea3e62. comments.concern: The constexpr constants of the hardware-attention header (hwkv_pages_per_layer, hwkv_tok_per_page, hwkv_pchannel_page_size_B and siblings) sit in the middle of the file; Wade asks to move them to the top so a reader can find them.

detection.procedure: For each touched header, list line numbers of `constexpr` definitions at namespace scope (grep -n 'constexpr' FILE at HEAD) and the line of the first function or struct body; flag constants defined after it. Check whether a config header for the same subsystem exists (h/pos/config.hpp) and whether another reviewer already asked for the move.
detection.question: Is a namespace-scope constant defined below the first function or struct of the file, so that a reader must search the file body to locate it?

comments.quote: kinda pedantic, but can we move all these constexpr to the top of this file :). It drives me nuts trying to (re)locate these sometimes, buried in the middle of the code like this
comments.note: Wade self-replied (2949458908) deferring to mcherba's request to move them into config.hpp. Author: 'fixed in commit 8a6db7243'. Verified: 8a6db72438 adds 6 lines to h/pos/config.hpp; at head 429249ead6 hwkv_tok_per_page and hwkv_pchannel_page_size_B are at h/pos/config.hpp:90-91 and hwattention.hpp:450 keeps only a comment naming them.

comments.concern: The shard constructor sizes each layer's HBM (FPGA high-bandwidth memory) allocation from the constant hwkv_pchannel_page_size_B = 8192, which Wade reads as a hidden assumption of 8 KV heads; he asks what happens with models that have more KV heads and whether the page size should be a parameter of the allocation scheme.

detection.trigger: An allocation or address computation in the diff multiplies a fixed constant (page size, stride, count) that is not derived from the model parameters (n_kv_heads, head_size) passed to the same function or constructor.
detection.procedure: Find the constant's definition (git grep 'NAME\s*=' HEAD -- h) and its comment; list the model parameters available in scope (constructor arguments, params struct); check whether any production path can vary the parameter the constant implicitly fixes (grep for n_kv_heads values in model plugins). Ask whether the constant is a hardware fact or a derived quantity.

comments.concern: The hunk adds clear_kv_complete() (a reset of the per-layer K/V completion bitmasks on a KV page) with a comment saying it is called between forward passes, and Wade finds no caller, so the completion flags would never be cleared.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a function (or any symbol) whose own comment or name says it resets, clears or releases state at some lifecycle point (between passes, on reuse, on free), and the diff contains no call to it.
detection.procedure: For every function the diff adds in h/ or src/, run `git grep -n '<name>(' HEAD -- h src bin` and exclude the definition line. For each added function with zero callers, read its comment: if the comment names a lifecycle point ('called between forward passes'), find the code that implements that lifecycle point (the forward-pass loop, the page-reuse path) and confirm nothing there performs the reset. Also check the stateful fields the function touches (k_complete_/v_complete_) for any other writer that clears them.
detection.question: Which production line clears this state at the lifecycle point the comment names, and if none does, what observes the stale state (here: is_kv_complete returning true for a reused page offset)?

comments.quote: how come I don't see this being called anywhere? We should be clearing these flags between forward passes right?
comments.note: Verified read-only at commit c459e255d9: kv_cache.hpp:560 defines clear_kv_complete() and `git grep clear_kv_complete` over h/ and src/ finds only that definition (no caller). The author's fix rejected the premise of the comment's second sentence: completion bits are per token per page and must persist until the offset is reused, so a per-pass clear would have been wrong; he replaced it with clear_kv_complete_at(offset), called from create_children and the single-token node constructor (head 1a88e897e1: kv_cache.hpp:557, full.hpp:524 and :568). So Wade's detection (no caller) was right and his proposed lifecycle (between forward passes) was wrong; the skill's rule 'concede the substance, correct the detail' applies. Check 6 fits only in theme (comment claims a behavior the code does not perform); check 6 as written triggers on compile-time rejection claims only, so it would not fire.

If a helper exists, the finding is 'replace with <helper>'; if the PR also introduces a new env var name, compare with the helper's variable name.

detection.trigger: A diff adds a hand-written loop that grows or fills a standard container (while size < n push_back(...), for-loop of push_back) next to, or in the same function as, an existing resize/assign call on a sibling container.

comments.concern: The new line computes pchan_size_bytes (the HBM pseudo-channel size in bytes) from a register field multiplied by the bare literals 1024 * 1024; Wade objects to unnamed magic numbers in general and files it as a clean-up item.

detection.trigger: An added production line (not test) contains a numeric literal other than 0 or 1 used in arithmetic or as an argument, with no named constant and no comment giving its meaning (here 1024 * 1024 as a MiB-to-bytes factor).
detection.procedure: Grep the diff's added lines in h/ and src/ for `[^0-9A-Za-z_]([2-9]|[1-9][0-9]+)[0-9]*` outside comments and strings; for each hit, read the statement and check whether a named constant with that meaning already exists (grep h/ for the value, e.g. `1024 \* 1024`, `MiB`, `MB`) or whether the surrounding names make the meaning obvious.
detection.question: Does a reader of this line know what the literal is (a unit factor, a hardware size, a count) without a name or comment?

comments.concern: The new TRON_ASSERT (the project's assertion macro, which takes a format string plus arguments) rejects a head_size not divisible by 8 but its message does not include the offending head_size value, so a failure log would not say which size tripped it.

detection.question: If this assertion fires in a log, can the reader recover the value that violated the condition from the message alone?

detection.procedure: Read the CMake hunk; grep CMakeLists.txt files for the same flags on other targets (e.g. `git grep -n 'mavx512' -- '*CMakeLists.txt'`) and for `target_link_libraries(... pos ...)` to find whether a dependent target already carried them PUBLIC; check which translation units in src/pos now include AVX intrinsics (grep `immintrin.h`, `_mm512`).
detection.question: Why did this target build before without these flags, and does the change make the dependency explicit or duplicate flags already inherited?

comments.concern: Wade restates, to confirm his understanding, the proposed change to DMA (direct memory access) transfer completion detection: large transfers span many descriptors, only the last descriptor's completion matters, and the existing xfer_k_entry_blocking()/xfer_v_entry_blocking() already do that but assume at most one descriptor-ring wrap, so the proposal is about the accuracy of 'done' under multiple wraps, not performance.

detection.trigger: A diff adds a prose design proposal (a multi-line comment starting 'Proposed change', a doc section, or a Note) describing a mechanism change in the DMA/descriptor/completion path without code.
detection.procedure: Read the proposal comment; find the current implementations it would replace (grep src/pos/driver.cpp for `wait_for_xfer_blocks`, `xfer_k_entry_blocking`, `xfer_v_entry_blocking`, `update_tail`, `wrap`) and state in one paragraph what they do today (which descriptor they wait on, how many ring wraps they tolerate); then write back the proposal as 'the goal is X, the difference from today is Y, this is about accuracy/performance, right?'.
detection.question: What does the current code assume (here: at most one ring wrap between enqueue and completion) that the proposed mechanism relaxes, and is the motivation correctness or speed?

comments.quote: I think the main difference is today, `xfer_k_entry_blocking()` and `xfer_v_entry_blocking()` assume at most **one wrap** between enqueue and completion time. But when we start sending much larger transfers, we may wrap **multiple** times.
comments.note: Wade had read the existing blocking transfer functions in driver.cpp (at 7362a5d245 wait_for_xfer_blocks is at :820 and ring-wrap handling at :1008-1046) and a prior verbal conversation ('our conversation on this'). Resolved by phone (his own reply 2026-01-20). He never commented on the doc/hw_attention.md content itself.

comments.concern: The staging-buffer free (free_staging_if_idle, which releases the GOF's two 8 KB host buffers whenever the in-flight DMA count reaches zero) is unconditional, so a workload that re-DMAs the same GOF repeatedly pays a full free + reallocate + repopulate (the 'swizzle', the data reordering into the hardware layout) each time with no hysteresis; he flags this as a possible performance regression to watch after merge.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a release/free of a reusable buffer or cache entry that fires on a counter reaching zero or on every completion event, with no delay, threshold, LRU or reuse check between the free and the next rebuild.
detection.procedure: Find the free function (grep for release_buffer, free_, evict, deallocate in the diff). Read its condition: is it only 'in-flight == 0'? Find every caller (grep the function name in src/ and h/) and the rebuild path (the function that reallocates and repopulates). Then list every production site that submits the same object again (grep the submit function: xfer_gof, backfill_shard, prepare_for_dma) and ask whether two submissions of the same object can occur close together (multi-shard fanout loops, speculation, retries). Estimate the rebuild cost from the repopulate function (does it copy and reorder the whole buffer?).
detection.question: Can the same object be freed and rebuilt repeatedly in steady state, and does the rebuild cost (copy + reorder) exceed the memory saved for that pattern?

comments.concern: A code comment (the new Note [GOF staging eviction]) cites a work-tracker item ('Story 2814'); he asks to drop the tracker reference from code comments and offers the reworded line as a suggestion block.

detection.trigger: An added or changed code comment (not the PR body) contains a work-tracker or review reference: 'Story N', 'ticket', 'JIRA', 'issue #', 'PR #', 'review round', 'as discussed with'.
detection.procedure: grep the added lines of the diff for 'Story', 'Ticket', 'JIRA', 'PR #', 'issue #', 'round' inside comment lines (// or /* ... */). For each hit, rewrite the sentence without the reference and check that the technical content still stands on its own.

comments.concern: A three-line comment above a Perfetto TRACE_EVENT (a tracing span) explains it as part of the staging-eviction feature and cites the feature Note; he says the comment is unnecessary and the trace span is a general-purpose event not tied to that Note.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a comment that attributes a general-purpose statement (a trace span, a log line, a counter, an assert) to the PR's feature by name or by 'See Note [feature]', while the statement itself would be equally valid without the feature.
detection.procedure: For each added comment that cites a Note or the PR's feature, read the statement it documents. Ask whether the statement's content names anything feature-specific (an identifier introduced by the PR). If the statement is a TRACE_EVENT, spdlog call, TRON_ASSERT or counter with a generic label (here 'gof_rodeo' with 'layer'), the comment's feature link is a justification of why the author added it, not a description of what it does. Propose deleting the comment or reducing it to what the statement does.
detection.question: If the feature were reverted, would this statement stay and still make sense, and would the comment then be wrong?

comments.concern: The new struct inflight_guard (an RAII credit holder) starts with an explicit 'public:' access specifier, which is the default for a struct and so redundant.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a 'struct X {' followed by 'public:' as the first access specifier, or a 'class X {' followed by 'private:' as the first specifier.
detection.procedure: grep -n -A1 '^struct .*{$' over the added lines and flag a following 'public:'; grep -n -A1 '^class .*{$' and flag a following 'private:'. Check that no earlier non-default specifier precedes it inside the same type.
detection.question: Is the first access specifier in this type the same as the keyword's default?

comments.concern: The address fix replaces a variable with the bare literal 4 in 'fetcher = (position / 4) % num_fetchers' (fetcher = which FPGA fetch unit owns a token position); he notes the file has many such unnamed numbers (4, 8, 32, 128) and asks for named definitions in one common location.

detection.trigger: An added or changed production line (h/ or src/, not t/) uses a bare integer literal other than 0 or 1 in arithmetic, an index, a shift, a mask or a size, with no named constant and no comment naming its meaning.
detection.procedure: grep the added production lines for '[^A-Za-z_0-9][2-9][0-9]*[^A-Za-z_0-9]' and '[0-9]x[0-9a-fA-F]+' outside comments and string literals. For each hit, search h/ for an existing named constant with the same value and meaning (grep the value with 'constexpr' or '#define' nearby, and grep the surrounding words such as 'fetcher', 'page', 'word'). If one exists, the finding is 'use the existing name'; if not, 'name it and put it next to the other hardware constants' (name the file where siblings live). Count the other bare literals in the same file to show the family.
detection.question: Can a reader at this line say what the literal measures (which hardware or layout quantity) without reading the author's head?

comments.concern: The new test prints the overall mismatch count unconditionally at info level, while the older tests in the same file print their mismatch count only when it is nonzero; he offers a suggestion block adding 'if (k_mm || v_mm)' and asks for consistency.

detection.trigger: A new TEST_CASE in an existing test file adds an unconditional spdlog::info/warn/error call that reports a count or result that the REQUIRE on the next line already checks, while sibling TEST_CASEs in the same file guard the equivalent print with 'if (count > 0)' or 'if (count)'.
detection.procedure: In the test file at HEAD, grep -n 'mismatch' (or the counter name) and read each print site with 3 lines of context. Record for each sibling whether the print is guarded. If the new unit differs from the file's pattern, propose the guard as a suggestion block. Also check the log level matches the siblings (error vs info).
detection.question: Does every other unit in this file print this kind of result only when it is nonzero, and does the new one print it always?

For each block, check whether a comment above it says why it is kept (a documented manual-debug switch). If not, ask for removal.

comments.concern: Cutting max_xfer_time_in_ns (the DMA transfer wait limit) from 10 s back to 100 ms will make the 'DMA XFER saw wait time of ... ns' log fire more often; Wade has already seen that log with the value 18446744073709551614 while loading oss-120b-tp4 on the branch and asks what it implies and whether main shows it too.

detection.trigger: A hunk lowers a timeout, poll count or other threshold constant in a header (here h/pos/config.hpp, labelled a 'debug-value revert' in the body).
detection.procedure: grep h/ and src/ for every reader of the constant; for each reader that logs or errors when the measured value exceeds it (here src/pos/driver.cpp:1058 `spdlog::debug("DMA XFER saw wait time of {} ns", etime)` under `if (etime > max_xfer_time_in_ns)`), state what the new limit does to that path; look for any recent log or run report that shows the measured values, and ask whether they exceed the new limit on main as well as on the branch.
detection.question: Which code path changes behavior when the measured value crosses the new, smaller limit, and do observed runtime values on the target branch already cross it?

comments.quote: With this reduction, I'm speculating we'll see a LOT more... not saying that's a reason to keep the larger value, but I wonder what it implies in our branch? Or do we see these in `main` too? Does anyone know?
comments.note: Code fact at 159e09a940: src/pos/driver.cpp:1055-1061 computes etime = ctime - stime from two TSC reads and logs the debug line the first time etime > max_xfer_time_in_ns. The logged value 18446744073709551614 is 2^64 - 2, i.e. a negative difference wrapped to unsigned. mcherba's reply (2026-05-21) says this comes from a paired TSC read where the second read was smaller than the first; the code logs it, copies the second value over the first and continues; max_xfer_time_in_ns does not affect it. So Wade's hypothesis (more logs because of the smaller limit) was refuted for the specific log he saw, but the question was answered rather than dismissed. He addressed two people (@mcherba, @BillBaumann), not only the author.

comments.concern: When a function (drain_reserves, the slab-cache drain in the DMA heap) is split into a traced wrapper and an untraced core, Wade thinks the original name should stay on the original body and the new wrapper should carry the new name (drain_reserved_traced), not the other way round.

detection.trigger: A hunk renames an existing function body to a `_untraced`/`_impl`/`_inner` variant and gives the original name to a new thin wrapper that adds instrumentation (TRACE_EVENT, logging, a counter).
detection.procedure: Read the hunk; list the callers of the original name (grep h/ src/ t/ for `drain_reserves(`); check whether the PR body states that existing callers should inherit the instrumentation; if it does, the direction is deliberate and the finding is at most a naming note; if not, ask which direction was intended.
detection.question: Should existing callers of the original name receive the new instrumentation transparently (keep the name on the wrapper), or opt in (new name on the wrapper)?

comments.concern: A new file-scope global MWAIT_C0 (the mwaitx C-state operand, 0xF << 4) is declared as a mutable uint32_t; Wade suggests making it const unless the value is meant to change at runtime.

detection.trigger: A hunk adds a namespace-scope or file-scope variable with an uppercase constant-style name, initialised from a literal expression, without const, constexpr or inline constexpr.
detection.procedure: grep the file and its includers for every write to the name (assignment, address taken, passed by non-const reference); if the only uses are reads, propose `const` (or `inline constexpr` per the project's header style) as a suggestion block.
detection.question: Is the variable ever written after initialisation, and if not, why is it not const?

comments.quote:
```suggestion
const uint32_t MWAIT_C0 = (0xF << 4);
```
that is... if we don't plan to ever change this value?
comments.note: Code fact at 08b5f10085: `uint32_t MWAIT_C0 = (0xF << 4);` sits at namespace tron::hardware::mwaitx scope with external linkage, next to `std::atomic<int> count_calls` and `bool MWAITX_SUPPORTED = is_supported();`. Its only uses are the two `"a"(MWAIT_C0)` asm input operands in for_event_cycles and indefinitely. The hunk moved an inline `uint32_t state = (0xF << 4);` local (with comment '0xF is (state=0) - 1') to this global. PR closed unmerged; no reply.

comments.concern: The function is named 'indefinitely' but it uses mwaitx with a timeout operand of 0xFFFFFFFF cycles, so each wait wakes after about 4 billion cycles rather than waiting forever; Wade asks whether a true indefinite wait would use mwait instead and whether the name is misleading.

detection.trigger: A hunk changes the body of a function whose name states a behavior (indefinitely, never, always, once, untraced) and the new body contains an operand, comment or branch that contradicts the name (here `options = 2; // Use timeout` next to `"b"(0xFFFFFFFF)); // No timeout`).
detection.procedure: Read the function body at HEAD; list each statement that bounds or conditions the behavior the name promises (a timeout operand, a loop bound, a capability check); for ISA operands, check the instruction reference (AMD mwaitx: ECX bit 1 enables the EBX timeout in TSC cycles); state whether the outer loop restores the promised behavior; then ask whether the name or the body should change.
detection.question: Does the function, as a whole, do what its name says, and if only because an outer loop re-enters, does the inline comment say so?

comments.quote: this function is named "indefinitely" but it's not _really_ waiting forever, right? A true indefinite wait would use "mwait" instead of "mwaitx", correct? This method is instead basically waiting 4 billion cycles, and then will time-out anyway
comments.note: Code fact at 08b5f10085 src/pos/mwaitx.cpp:69-85: `static void indefinitely(volatile uint64_t* trigger, auto condition)` loops `while (!condition(*trigger))`; inside, when MWAITX_SUPPORTED, it executes monitorx then `uint32_t options = 2; // Use timeout` and `mwaitx` with `"c"(options), "b"(0xFFFFFFFF)); // No timeout`. The two comments contradict each other on the same instruction. Because the outer while loop re-enters after each wake, the function does wait until the condition holds (indefinite as a whole), but each mwaitx sleep is bounded at 2^32 TSC cycles (about 1 to 2 s at 2 to 4 GHz). Wade's claim that it 'will time-out anyway' is right per instruction and wrong per function. Also, when MWAITX_SUPPORTED is false (the Granite Rapids case this PR is for), the loop is a pure busy spin. Addressed to @BillBaumann, not the PR author, and framed as a learning question ('newby-probe here :)'). PR closed unmerged; no reply.

detection.trigger: A hunk adds a runtime guard that silently no-ops or returns on a condition the surrounding comment or design says cannot happen: `if (this != &other)` in a move/copy assignment, a null check with early return on a pointer that is never null, a bounds clamp on an index computed by the same class.
detection.procedure: List every added conditional whose false branch does nothing or returns. For each, read the comment that justifies the operation (here 'Move constructor - needed because atomics are not movable') and grep callers for the operation (`std::move(` of the type, `operator=` uses, vector reallocation of the type). If no caller can reach the condition, ask whether an assert, or deleting the operation, is the better contract.
detection.question: Is there a legitimate caller that reaches this condition, or should the condition be asserted or the operation deleted?

comments.concern: Objects to adding an unbounded spin-wait on wqentry::in_flight (a per-work-request busy flag cleared by the hardware completion callback): it replaces a loud assertion with a silent hang when the completion path is stuck, duplicates the backpressure the rxinfo_ring (receive-descriptor ring) already provides, and may be masking a different root cause (a false completion on matmul_rx_q feeding a stale scratchpad).

detection.trigger: the diff adds a loop that polls an atomic or flag with no timeout, no iteration bound and no abort, on a path where the flag is cleared by an asynchronous completion callback; or the diff removes or bypasses a TRON_ASSERT on the same condition
detection.procedure: grep the diff for `while (` or `for (;;)` around `.load(` / `in_flight` / `_pause()` without a deadline; find who clears the flag (grep the store of the flag with release ordering) and whether that clearer runs on an RX/worker thread that can itself be stuck; read the function the wait is inserted into (hw_prepare, fill) for an existing ordering guarantee (ring-overflow check at the top, head/tail backpressure); check `git log -S<flag>` for an earlier assert on the same condition and for an earlier reverted attempt of the same wait
detection.question: when the completion callback never fires, does the new code hang silently where the old code asserted, and does an existing ring backpressure already serialize the reuse this wait is meant to prevent?

detection.procedure: read every added comment block in the diff; for each notation token (regex `Q\.?\d+`, `Q\d+\.\d+`), compare the integer-bit count it implies with the integer-bit count the surrounding sentences state; also compare with identifier suffixes (`_q61`) and assert messages that spell the same format
detection.question: does the notation as written mean what the surrounding comment says it means?

detection.question: does every literal bound to this setting name now agree with the new default, and for each one that differs, is it a deliberate fallback for a different build path?

comments.concern: Answering another reviewer's question about thread safety under the new parallel loader: alloc_hardware_weights (the HBM allocator call) is already mutex-protected, but set_hardware_weights (the per-device DMA weight transfer) is not, so concurrent calls on the same PosDevice (one FPGA card object) would race on its load_weight_q DMA queue.

detection.trigger: The diff introduces or widens parallel execution (parallel_for, new threads, a worker fanout) around a call that reaches a shared mutable resource (a device queue, a descriptor ring, a hardware handle).
detection.procedure: Follow every call inside the new parallel region to its definition (here h/tron/hardware/tensor.hpp -> src/pos/driver.cpp set_hardware_weights). For each shared object it touches (dev->load_weight_q, allocator), grep its definition and the function body for a std::mutex, lock_guard or atomic; note which calls are protected and which are not. Check whether two parallel iterations can map to the same device/queue instance.
detection.question: Can two iterations of the new parallel loop reach the same mutable shared object, and does every function on that path take a lock before mutating it?

comments.quote: But `set_hardware_weights` is not. So concurrent accesses on the *same* PosDevice would contend on (e.g.) `load_weight_q` DmaQueue with no lock/guard protection.
comments.note: Verified at b556b55: h/pos/alloc.hpp:136 `mutable std::mutex mutex_` backs allocator::allocate (Wade's 'is thread-safe (uses a mutex)' holds); src/pos/driver.cpp:1007-1024 set_hardware_weights(PosDevice*) does xfer_blocks(dev, dev->load_weight_q, ...) then wait_for_xfer_blocks with no lock (Wade's 'is not' holds). The author then added hardware_weight_load_mutex(dev_idx) and a lock_guard in tensor.hpp:66-71 and :93 (present at b556b55, which Wade critiques in 3277240111). Wade's wording: fact first, 'So' consequence second. Reply to axch, but the content is a finding, not a social answer.

comments.concern: The new per-device mutex is taken at the caller (a free-floating mutex array in tensor.hpp) rather than inside the object it protects (PosDevice or its DmaQueue), so the lock is far from the protected state, spans more than needed (the busy-wait in wait_for_xfer_blocks could run concurrently), fully serializes parallel callers, and future callers of the same queue can forget it; he also worries about adding a mutex to a hot path, and defers to the driver owner.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a mutex, lock_guard or lock table in a file other than the one that defines the mutated object, or adds a lock around a call whose body contains both the mutation and a wait/poll.
detection.procedure: Locate the object the lock protects (grep the callee for the member it mutates: here dev->load_weight_q in src/pos/driver.cpp:1022). List every other caller of that mutation (grep xfer_blocks / load_weight_q in h/ src/) and check whether each would also need the new lock. Read the callee body and split it into the mutating part (xfer_blocks) and the read-only waiting part (wait_for_xfer_blocks, driver.cpp:966-994, reads q->consumed_head and monotonic descriptor indices); ask whether the lock span could end after the mutating part. Check whether the device object already owns mutexes for sibling resources (h/pos/device.hpp: qalloc_mutex, hw_prepare_mutex, wcmd_post_mutex) that show the house convention.
detection.question: Does the lock live with the state it protects, cover only the mutating section, and get taken by every path that mutates that state?

comments.quote: this sort of free-floating lock placement is detached from what it's actually protecting. IMO it would be better to add a mutex member to the PosDevice (or DmaQueue) and use it directly inside of `device::set_hardware_weights`.
comments.note: Verified: tensor.hpp:66-71 at b556b55 defines `static std::array<std::mutex, MAX_DEVICES> mutexes` in a free function; tensor.hpp:93 takes it around the whole device call; driver.cpp:1021-1023 = xfer_blocks then wait_for_xfer_blocks; wait_for_xfer_blocks only reads q->consumed_head->fields.desc_idx and compares with start/end descriptors (monotonic, per-range), matching Wade's point 2. h/pos/device.hpp already holds qalloc_mutex / hw_prepare_mutex / wcmd_post_mutex as members (house convention supports his ask). Four numbered reasons, then a counter-consideration ('nervous about introducing mutex locks in high-volume functions'), then 'probably fine ... may be acceptable', then deferral to @mcherba. No reply in the digest; PR still open, so outcome unknown.

comments.concern: A markdown line in the added docs is far longer than the file's wrap width, and he asks why the project formatter (`make format`) did not catch it, guessing it does not process markdown.

detection.trigger: An added or changed line in a .md file is much longer than the surrounding lines of the same file (here 144 columns in a file wrapped at about 90).
detection.procedure: For each changed .md file, compute the max line length of added lines versus the median of unchanged lines (awk over the diff). Check GNUmakefile `format` target and lefthook.yml for which file types the formatter covers; if markdown is not covered, the finding is a manual rewrap plus the fact that no tool guards it.
detection.question: Is any added documentation line wider than the file's existing wrap width, and would the repository formatter have caught it?
