comments.concern: He approves the PR as read, then pastes four items from a Claude review he ran (fragile copy of Perfetto internal macros with no version pin; emission sites that bypass the gating header; undocumented single-writer assumption on process-global relaxed atomics; help-text gap for per-generation pass renumbering) as optional follow-ups with 'some merit'.

detection.trigger: The PR copies or overrides a third-party library's internal macros or relies on process-global mutable state; or more generally the PR is large and Wade has read it without findings of his own.
detection.procedure: Run an agent review of the diff; for each item classify: (a) copied upstream implementation -> check for a version/commit pin in the comment and a runtime test that exercises the override (grep '#undef' + 'PERFETTO_INTERNAL' in h/common/perfetto.hpp, grep the test for an assertion that a real emitted slice is suppressed); (b) a gate implemented in one header -> grep the tree for direct includes of the upstream header that bypass it (grep -rn 'include <perfetto' h/ src/ excluding the gating header); (c) process-global atomics with relaxed ordering -> look for a comment stating the single-writer invariant; (d) documented behaviour (README) absent from `--help` text -> diff README claims against the CLI usage string.
detection.question: Which agent-review items name a real mechanism (version drift, bypass path, undocumented invariant, help/README mismatch), and are they worth a follow-up rather than a block?

comments.concern: Part 1 of 2 (same comment id): the PR body calls `--trace-passes` a 'Perfetto option', but it is a runtron (the command-line inference driver) option that guides Perfetto (the tracing library) instrumentation; he asks the author to confirm and calls it a nit.

comments.concern: Part 2 of 2 (same comment id): most developers launch Perfetto through the wrapper script perfetto/tronperf, which forwards options to runtron, so a new runtron option is incomplete until the wrapper accepts and forwards it too.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a command-line option, environment variable or config knob to a binary that the repository also drives through a wrapper or launcher script (perfetto/tronperf, perfetto/wrapper, bin/*.sh, ci scripts).
detection.procedure: grep the new flag string across perfetto/, bin/, ci/, packaging/ and README files; list every launcher that forwards other options of the same binary (grep for an existing sibling flag such as --trace-gen in perfetto/tronperf) and check whether the new flag appears there too, including its usage/help text.
detection.question: Does every wrapper script that forwards sibling options to this binary also accept and forward the new option?

comments.quote: The majority of runtron developers (if not all) use the perfetto/tronperf script to launch Perfetto against runtron. So that script needs an update to take this new parameter, and forward it to runtron (like it does other options today)

comments.concern: A test asserts a hard-coded SHA256 digest over reference checkpoint arrays; he asks where the value came from, whether its provenance is documented, and whether it belongs in the repository's evidence register docs/ANCHORED_EVIDENCE.md (which the AGENTS doc points to).

detection.trigger: A test hunk adds an equality assertion against a long opaque literal (a hash hex string, a digest, a checksum, a frozen float table) with no comment or document naming how it was produced.
detection.procedure: For each opaque literal in added test lines (regex for 32+ hex characters or long numeric tables), grep docs/ and AGENTS.md / CLAUDE.md for the literal and for an evidence or provenance register the repository mandates; read the nearest comment above the assertion; check whether the PR body or docs name the generating command, date and source revision. Ask for the registration if the repository has a register.
detection.question: Can a reader regenerate or trace this literal from a documented source, and is it registered where the repository says such frozen evidence must be listed?

comments.quote: is this crazy 'magic' digest/sha captured/documented anywhere? Where did it come from? Are these supposed to be listed in the ANCHORED_EVIDENCE doc (I just happened to see that referenced from the AGENTS doc)

The literal is a SHA256 over all D128 checkpoint arrays of the tiny chunked_stress native reference, frozen 2026-09-11 from the v1 NumPy reference, kept as a regression lock across v2/v3. Wade found the register rule by reading the repo's AGENTS doc, i.e. he reads project policy files before commenting.

comments.concern: The spec introduces the term 'safe mode' (the interpreter validating a full program set before writing to hardware) for the first time with no definition and no link to where it is described or how it is selected.

detection.trigger: An added prose line uses a quoted or capitalised mode/feature name (here 'safe mode') that does not appear elsewhere in the file before this line and has no link, footnote or parenthetical definition.
detection.procedure: For each distinctive term in added documentation lines, grep the file at HEAD for earlier occurrences and for a link target; grep the rest of the docs tree and the referenced code repositories for a section that defines it. If the first occurrence is in the diff and no pointer exists, ask for a definition or a link, naming what a reader needs (how it is enabled, disabled, chosen).
detection.question: Is this the term's first appearance, and does the text give the reader a definition or a pointer to where the mechanism is described?

comments.quote: first mention of 'safe mode'... is there a link/reference pointer to where this is better described (e.g. how it's enabled/disabled/dictated/driven)?

comments.concern: Wade endorses the Cursor Bugbot high-severity finding that narrowing token_ix_needed to a single mask range lets a minibatch stop waiting for a later minibatch writing V entries on the same shared KV page, while scaled_v still reads the whole page (interleaved storage, zero times NaN corrupts), and asks (via pasted GPT text) to keep waiting for every writer of a read page and to extend t_llama_unit coverage for shared-page readiness.

detection.trigger: A hunk narrows or removes a readiness, dependency or wait predicate (a function whose name contains needed, ready, visible, depends, wait) on a path where another thread or minibatch writes into shared storage that the consumer reads at a coarser granularity (whole page, whole cache line, interleaved pair).
detection.procedure: Read the old and new predicate (common.hpp:1003-1012 at 92ff9b9e49: page-level `find_range(page.at_offset(0))` loop replaced by one `find_range(tok).any_visible(items_mask)`). Find the consumer's read granularity: grep `scaled_v` and the V accessor in h/tron/models/kv_cache.hpp for whether it reads a full page including masked-out entries, and whether even/odd tokens share storage (the interleaved V layout). Construct the case: a prompt split into two minibatches sharing one 64-token page, where the second batch's tokens are causally invisible to the first. Then check whether an existing test pre-initializes all V data (which hides the race) and whether any test covers shared-page readiness. The PR body at the merged head confirms the mechanism: 'Restoring only the old producer-token visibility predicate makes both shared-page readiness cases fail'.
detection.question: After the narrowing, can a consumer read storage (a page, an interleaved pair) that a writer the consumer no longer waits for is still writing?

detection.procedure: Read the callee at the same commit (common.hpp:804-822 at af295981ea: `for (size_t pi = 0; pi < passes.size(); ++pi) for (hw_query const& query : pass.queries)`), and the loop above the call site (model.hpp:2651-2657: `for (size_t i = 0; i < passes.size(); ++i) ... for (auto const& query : pass.queries) ... prepare_raw_result(query.job_ix)`). comments.concern: Wade approves as-is but asks whether the author considered publishing the page-share counters through FUSE (the server's live statistics file interface) with env-var opt-in, so they could be read while the process runs and measured over chosen intervals instead of as a compile-time option printed at process exit.

detection.trigger: The diff adds a new counter, histogram or diagnostic that is enabled by a compile-time option (CMake option, #ifdef) and reported once (stderr print at exit, log line, destructor of a static), in a code base that already has a runtime statistics interface (grep h/ and src/ for the stats/FUSE publishing layer, e.g. `attn_stats`, `set_value`, README.stats.md).

If the existing mechanism gives all three for the same counters, write the finding as a question with the two alternatives and state it is not a condition of approval.

comments.concern: Wade argues that adding explicit `= 0` / `= false` / `= nullptr` initializers to every PosDevice member is pedantic because, by the C++ value-initialization rule he cites from PR 2301, `new object()` already zero-initializes members without initializers once any default member initializer exists; he approves anyway because being explicit is good.

detection.trigger: A PR adds a mechanical, whole-file safety change (explicit initializers, redundant qualifiers, duplicated checks) whose stated reason is a guarantee the language or an existing declaration already provides.
detection.procedure: Read the PR body's stated reason (here: 'standardizing on default initialization everywhere ... better to be explicit' from PR 2193). Find how objects of the type are created (`new PosDevice(`, braces, constructor) and whether the class has a user-provided constructor (gh pr diff 2438 shows `PosDevice(int index, ...` in device.hpp). State the language rule that applies, cite the earlier PR where the team discussed it, and grade the change as redundant-but-harmless or needed.
detection.question: Does the language rule for how this type is constructed already give the guarantee the change adds, and if so is the change still wanted for explicitness?

comments.quote: I think what we are doing here is a bit pedantic (in latest C++ standards, once a struct 'object' has any default member initializer, 'new object()' triggers value-initialization of the whole object, which zero-initializes all members without explicit initializers...
comments.note: Full review body also says 'sorry @hvaneenoo-positron, been heads down in AoF land lately' and ends '... but I also think that being explicit is a good thing :-). Approved.' with a link to PR 2301's description. PR still open (head fc4fc8780a), no author reply in the digest.
